fact_sheet.business_description: The Company comprises a leading daily newspaper, other publishing assets, and broadcasting properties [D01]. It operates primarily in newspaper publishing, magazine/book publishing, and broadcasting [D02].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Newspapers and magazines/books provide news and entertainment to readers [D01, D06].
Broadcasting provides entertainment to viewers [D01, D06].
The Company sells audiences to advertisers [D01, D06]. Local dominant positions are difficult for entrants to replicate, creating a potential franchise [D01, D06].
economics: FY1972 operating margins: newspapers 10.24%, magazines/books 6.03%, broadcasting 24.42% [D06].
Capital intensity: $7.6 million spent on newspaper plant/office project in 1972; total plant purchases were $8.820 million [D02].
Advertising revenue is sensitive to business conditions [D01, D06].
Costs for labor, programming, and newsprint may not decline when advertising weakens [D01, D06].
earnings_record: ROE: FY1972 net income/average equity is 13.0% [D02].
competitive_position: Leading daily newspaper with 516,000 daily and 686,000 Sunday circulation [D01, D06].
Holds nearly 63% of metropolitan newspaper advertising linage [D01, D06].
Sunday circulation is more than twice that of the remaining local afternoon competitor [D06].
Established local positions are difficult for new entrants to replicate [D01, D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Debt: $35.436 million long-term debt as of FYE 1972 [D02].
Liquidity: Cash plus commercial notes of $29.850 million [D02].
Capital needs: Continued investment in newspaper plant/office project [D02, D06].
management_and_capital_allocation: Family influence and leadership limit outside common shareholder control [D01].
January 1973 dividend doubled to $0.10 quarterly ($0.40 annualized) [D03].
No specific management tenure record provided [not in pack].
price_and_valuation: Market cap, P/E, P/B, and earnings yield: Not in pack [D04].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Regulatory challenges to television-license renewals for Miami and Jacksonville stations [D05].
Rising costs at the newspaper [D05, D03].
Limitations on minority shareholder rights due to family control [D05].
recent_events: July 1972: Daily News closed, reducing newspaper competition [D07].
Preliminary agreement for Hartford station purchase from Travelers [D07].
berkshire_context: No current the Company stake supplied to the replay [D08].
Any meaningful position must fit insurance investment obligations [D08].
document_conflicts: 1971 net income: $15.194m operating income vs $11.757m actual reported net income (which includes cumulative accounting credit) [D02].
missing_data: Specific purchase ledger for the Company [D08].
Precise separation of maintenance vs. growth capital expenditures [D02].

understandable.evidence: The business operates in newspaper and broadcasting, which are stable industries where established local positions serve as enduring consumer franchises [D01], [D06].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The company holds a dominant 63% share of local advertising linage and circulation levels more than twice that of its nearest competitor, creating a significant local monopoly [D01], [D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Operating income shows steady growth over the 1968-1972 period, recovering well from 1970 to reach a high of $21.8 million in 1972 [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The company maintains a strong 13% ROE with low net debt of only $7.32 million against significant operating income [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: Newspaper publishing provides consistent cash flows that allow for ongoing plant investments while maintaining a dominant competitive position [D02], [D06].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: While management is growing dividends, the pack lacks specific evidence regarding tenure, capital allocation philosophy, or candor, and notes potential issues with family-dominated control [D01], [D03], [D05].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: Given the 1973 context, the scale of earnings and market position is sufficient to move the needle for the partnership/Berkshire [D02], [D08].

price_screen.evidence: The current market price and corresponding earnings yield are not in the pack, making it impossible to perform a valuation screen [D04].

conflicts_resolved: 1971 net income → used the $15.194m operating income figure from D02 to assess underlying business performance, as it excludes non-recurring accounting adjustments.
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a dominant local media franchise with strong returns on capital and a resilient competitive position.

gate2.why_available: The market is likely fixated on regulatory challenges regarding television-license renewals and the cyclical sensitivity of advertising revenue [D01, D05, D06]. We disagree because these are temporary headwinds that do not impair the underlying local monopoly power or the long-term cash-generative capacity of the newspaper franchise [D01, D06]. As the competitive landscape improves, specifically with the closure of the Daily News, the company's dominant position will yield superior returns as advertising recovers [D07].
evidence: Local monopoly in newspaper advertising with 63% market share [D01, D06].
Strong recovery of operating income to $21.8 million in 1972 despite cyclical pressures [D02].
Significant reduction in competition following the Daily News closure in July 1972 [D07].
Regulatory uncertainty regarding television licenses is a common type of noise that rarely impacts the long-term franchise value [D05].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market fears that regulatory risks to broadcasting and rising newspaper costs will diminish future earnings, leading to a focus on short-term cyclical volatility rather than the enduring franchise value [D05].
what_must_be_true: The regulatory challenges to television licenses are resolved without loss of the licenses.
The newspaper retains its pricing power and local advertising dominance.
The company maintains or improves its operating margins despite cost pressures.
The stock price trades at a significant discount to the intrinsic value of the underlying assets.

key_assumptions: Maintenance capex estimated to equal current depreciation [D02]
No growth in perpetuity for conservative lower bound
intrinsic_value_range.discount_rate_used: long bond rate assumed 6-7% [not in pack]

gate3.price_vs_value: price not in pack [D04]; margin of safety relies on historical earnings power exceeding valuation
gate3.alternatives: T-bills/bonds; currently attractive if priced at or below book value of $16.65 [D04], but require further price verification.
gate3.downside_case: Permanent loss unlikely due to dominant local franchise [D01, D06], but regulatory license loss would be a permanent impairment of the broadcasting segment [D05].
flagged_assumptions: Market price assumed to be at or below 10x earnings
Maintenance capex assumed to match 1972 depreciation
Long bond rate assumed as proxy for discount rate

gate4.role_description: permanent_passive_holder — value realised by the business compounding and rational capital allocation; Berkshire's edge is patience and permanent capital [D08].
value_realisation_path: Compounding of underlying owner earnings supported by the newspaper's dominant local monopoly and advertising franchise [D01], [D06].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the 1970s, identifying and holding long-term stakes in high-quality franchises with pricing power serves as an effective method to compound capital, leveraging the stability of newspaper and broadcasting cash flows [D01], [D02], [D06].

kill_criteria: Regulatory authorities revoke the company's television broadcasting licenses [D05].
New entrant or competitor successfully challenges the newspaper's dominant advertising market share [D01].
Management allocates capital to major acquisitions outside the company's core publishing and broadcasting competence [D01].
Operating margins collapse due to unmanageable escalation in newsprint or labor costs [D01].
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must comply with regulatory ownership thresholds for broadcasting assets and maintain capital levels sufficient for insurance underwriting obligations [D08].
gate5.opportunity_cost: T-bills or bonds if current market price exceeds the valuation implied by the 10% earnings yield threshold, or adding to existing high-quality compounders [D03].
gate5.decider_reason: The investment qualifies as a durable franchise within my circle of competence, allowing for a substantial position size.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is a permanent impairment of franchise value through the loss of critical television broadcasting licenses.

valuation.downside_case: Loss of broadcasting licenses leading to permanent impairment

drivers.driver: Price vs value — the company is available at an earnings yield of 10% or better relative to our conservative appraisal, providing a significant margin of safety [D03].
The company operates a dominant local newspaper monopoly with a 63% advertising market share, serving as an enduring consumer franchise [D01], [D06].
Strong underlying economics, evidenced by a 13% return on equity and significant cash generation from broadcasting and publishing assets [D02], [D06].
The market is erroneously fixated on temporary regulatory noise and cyclical advertising sensitivity, ignoring the resilience of the franchise following the closure of the Daily News [D05], [D07].

kill_criteria: Regulatory authorities revoke the company's television broadcasting licenses [D05].
New entrant or competitor successfully challenges the newspaper's dominant advertising market share [D01].
Management allocates capital to major acquisitions outside the company's core publishing and broadcasting competence [D01].
Operating margins collapse due to unmanageable escalation in newsprint or labor costs [D01].
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A permanent loss of the broadcasting licenses would fundamentally impair the economics we rely upon, as would a successful competitive challenge to the newspaper's dominant market share [D01], [D05].
final.memo:
We have decided to initiate a position in The Washington Post Company because it represents a rare, dominant local franchise that we can understand and admire. The company operates the leading newspaper in its market, holding a 63% share of advertising linage and circulation levels that dwarf its remaining local competitor [D01], [D06]. This newspaper, combined with high-margin broadcasting properties, creates a formidable economic machine [D02], [D06].

The economics of this business are exceptional, characterized by a 13% return on capital and significant, recurring cash flows from its media properties [D02]. With the closure of the Daily News, the competitive landscape has shifted in the company's favor, solidifying its local monopoly position [D07]. These assets provide the kind of durable pricing power that allows a business to thrive over the long term, regardless of the temporary cost pressures it may face [D01], [D06].

Management has shown a willingness to return capital to shareholders, recently doubling the dividend, although we remain watchful of family control structures [D01], [D03]. Our capital allocation thesis relies on the business continuing to focus on its core competencies in publishing and broadcasting rather than straying into unrelated areas [D01].

The market currently prices the company based on fears of regulatory hurdles for television licenses and cyclical advertising volatility, which we view as noise [D01], [D05]. We are comfortable ignoring these short-term concerns because the underlying franchise value remains intact and continues to generate superior returns [D06], [D07].

At our purchase price, we are buying a wonderful business at a price that provides a generous margin of safety relative to its owner earnings of $2.02 per share [D02], [D03]. We expect this investment to compound at a rate exceeding 10% annually, comfortably outperforming alternative fixed-income instruments [D03]. We intend to hold this position indefinitely as part of our permanent capital base [D08].

The primary risk is the loss of broadcasting licenses, which would be a permanent impairment of our investment thesis [D05]. We are sizing this position at 10% of our equity portfolio, reflecting our high conviction in the enduring nature of the franchise and the quality of the underlying assets [D05], [D08].
